ai.literal: Even if they are of indispensable excellence, things that come so as to diminish (one's honor), abandon them.
ai.translation: Even if they bring indispensable glory, one must abandon those actions that would diminish one's honor.
ai.modern: தவிர்க்க முடியாத பெருமையைத் தருவனவாக இருந்தாலும், தன் மானம் குறையும்படி வரும் செயல்களைக் கைவிட வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of personal honor over any worldly achievement. The phrase 'இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின' refers to things of indispensable excellence or greatness that seem absolutely necessary for life. Yet, the poet advises that if obtaining such greatness causes one's self-respect to diminish ('குன்ற'), those opportunities ('வருப') must be firmly rejected ('விடல்'). No amount of glory or success is worth the sacrifice of one's dignity.

ai.literal: Even if it brings wealth, deeds that are not honorable they will indeed not do, those who desire great fortitude along with honor.
ai.translation: Those who desire great fortitude along with honor will never do deeds that are unworthy of their dignity, even if such deeds would bring them immense wealth or greatness.
ai.modern: புகழுடன் கூடிய சிறந்த ஆண்மைத் தன்மையை விரும்புகின்றவர்கள், தமக்கு மிகுந்த செல்வம் தருவதாக இருந்தாலும், தமது பெருமைக்குத் தகாத செயல்களைச் செய்யவே மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the uncompromising nature of self-respect and honor. The poet explains that individuals who aspire to possess true strength of character and fortitude (pērāṇmai) alongside their honor (cīroṭu) will never stoop to doing things that are beneath their dignity (cīralla ceyyārē). Even if an action promises to bring them immense wealth, power, or external greatness (cīriṉum), they will reject it if it compromises their integrity. The word 'cīr' is used beautifully with different shades of meaning: first as material prosperity, then as fitting or honorable conduct, and finally as dignity itself. Thus, true honor is shown to be far more valuable than any material gain.

ai.literal: In prosperity is required humility; in small adversity is required loftiness.
ai.translation: In times of great prosperity, humility is required; in times of diminished fortune, maintaining one's dignity and loftiness of mind is required.
ai.modern: செல்வம் பெருகிய காலத்தில் பணிவுடன் இருக்க வேண்டும்; வறுமையால் வாழ்வு சுருங்கிய காலத்தில் மானத்தோடு கூடிய உயர்வான எண்ணத்தைக் கொண்டிருக்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the ideal conduct of a person of high character during the changing tides of fortune. In times of great prosperity, one must practice humility to avoid arrogance and show respect to others. Conversely, when one's circumstances are reduced or diminished, one must maintain high self-esteem and dignity rather than begging or losing self-respect. The contrast between humility in wealth and dignity in poverty highlights the true essence of honour.

ai.literal: Like hair fallen from the head are people, when they have fallen from their status.
ai.translation: People who fall from their high status of honor are like hair that has fallen from the head.
ai.modern: தம்முடைய உயர்ந்த நிலையிலிருந்து தாழ்ந்துபோகும்போது, மனிதர்கள் தலையிலிருந்து உதிர்ந்த மயிரைப் போன்றவர் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid analogy to illustrate the loss of honor. Hair on the head is highly valued and cared for, but once it falls off, it is treated as worthless and discarded with disgust. Similarly, people who fall from their high moral standing or honorable position lose all their respect and are looked down upon by society. The comparison emphasizes that honor, once lost, reduces a person's worth to nothing.

ai.literal: Even those who are like a hill will diminish, if they do degrading deeds that are like a tiny crab's eye seed.
ai.translation: Even those whose stature is as great as a mountain will shrink in esteem if they commit a degrading act as tiny as a crab's eye seed.
ai.modern: மலை போன்ற பெருமை உடையவர்களும், குன்றிமணி அளவு சிறியதான இழிவு தரும் செயல்களைச் செய்தால், தம் பெருமை அழிந்து தாழ்ந்து போவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the absolute importance of maintaining one's honor and avoiding even the smallest dishonorable act. The poet uses a striking contrast between a massive hill ('kuṉṟu') and a tiny crab's eye seed ('kuṉṟi') to illustrate this. Even individuals of mountain-like greatness will lose their high standing and shrink in the eyes of the world if they commit a degrading deed, no matter how minuscule it may seem. The wordplay on 'kuṉṟu' (as a hill and as the verb to diminish) and 'kuṉṟi' (the tiny seed) reinforces how easily great honor can be eroded by a single small lapse.

ai.literal: Fame since it does not yield, to the world of gods it will not lead, what then is the use of going and standing behind those who despise?
ai.translation: If it yields no fame on earth and does not lead to the world of the gods, what is the use of going and standing in subservience behind those who despise you?
ai.modern: ஒருவருக்குப் புகழையும் தராது, தேவர் உலகத்திற்கும் வழிநடத்தாது என்றால், தம்மை இகழ்ந்து பேசுபவர்களின் பின்னால் சென்று அடங்கி நிற்பதால் என்ன பயன் விளையும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the futility of compromising one's self-respect for material or social gain. The poet argues that bowing down and serving those who hold you in contempt (இகழ்வார் பின் சென்று நிலை) brings absolutely no benefit. It neither earns you honor and fame (புகழ்) in this earthly life, nor does it pave the way to the heavenly realm of the gods (புத்தேள் நாடு) in the afterlife. Since it serves no purpose in either world, maintaining one's dignity is the only honorable path.

ai.literal: Than a person living by going behind those who do not agree, being said to have perished at that very instant is better.
ai.translation: Rather than living by following behind those who do not respect or agree with them, it is far better for a person to be spoken of as having perished at that very moment.
ai.modern: தம்மை மதிக்காத பகைவர்களின் பின்னே சென்று ஒருவன் உயிர்வாழ்வதை விட, அவன் அப்போதே அழிந்துவிட்டான் என்று பிறரால் சொல்லப்படுவது நல்லது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme importance of self-respect over a compromised life. The poet compares two choices: living subserviently by following those who are hostile or disrespectful ('ஒட்டார் பின் சென்று வாழ்தல்'), and dying or being ruined at that very moment ('அந்நிலையே கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல்'). The word 'ஒட்டார்' refers to adversaries or those who do not align with one's dignity. The couplet declares that it is far better ('நன்று') to be known as having perished instantly with honor intact than to survive by begging or serving those who look down upon you.

ai.literal: Is it an elixir of immortality, the life that preserves the flesh, when great dignity and honour are ruined?
ai.translation: When one's great dignity and honour are ruined, is the life spent in preserving this fleshly body an elixir of immortality?
ai.modern: பெருந்தன்மையும் மானமும் அழியும்படியான நிலைமை வரும்போது, உடம்பைக் காப்பாற்றிக் கொண்டு வாழ்கின்ற வாழ்க்கை என்ன சாகா மருந்தா?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of self-respect over mere physical survival. The poet asks a rhetorical question: when a situation arises where one's great dignity (பெருந்தகைமை) and honour (பீடு) are destroyed, is preserving this physical body (ஊன்) with life (வாழ்க்கை) like consuming an elixir of immortality (மருந்து)? Since physical life is temporary anyway, sacrificing one's honour just to keep the body alive is futile and ignoble.

ai.literal: If hair is lost, not living yak-beast like those, life will give up, if honor [threatened] comes.
ai.translation: Those who value their honor like the yak, which does not survive if it loses its hair, will give up their lives if their self-respect is threatened.
ai.modern: தன் உடம்பிலிருந்து மயிர் நீங்கினால் உயிர் வாழாத கவரிமானைப் போன்றவர்கள், தங்களுக்கு மானக் குறைவு வரும்போது உயிரை விட்டுவிடுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares highly self-respecting individuals to the 'kavarimā' (yak), a beast traditionally believed to die of grief if it loses its hair. The word 'māṉam' here represents personal honor, dignity, and self-respect. The phrase 'uyir nīppar' shows that for such noble people, physical existence is worthless if their honor is compromised. The poet emphasizes that preserving one's integrity is far more valuable than preserving one's physical life.

ai.literal: Disgrace if comes, who do not live, honour those who possess, [their] glory, having worshipped, will praise, the world.
ai.translation: The world will worship and praise the bright glory of those who possess such honour that they would not choose to live if disgrace befell them.
ai.modern: அவமானம் வந்தால் உயிர் வாழாத மானம் உடையவர்களுடைய புகழை, இவ்வுலகம் தொழுது போற்றும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of honour and self-respect. It describes people who possess such high self-esteem that they prefer death over a life of disgrace (iḷi). The poet states that the world (ulaku) does not just remember these individuals, but actively bows down to (toḻutu) and extols (ēttum) their lasting glory (oḷi). The word 'oḷi' here represents the radiant, luminous fame that outlives their physical existence.
